newsitem.title: FRANCE: French potato futures market loses appeal.
newsitem.headline: French potato futures market loses appeal.

text.p: Potato futures, which produced stunning profits for speculators in the mid-1990s, are being wound up in Paris this month through lack of interest.

The ordinary Bintje potato, whose price rocketed by more than five times after a bad harvest in 1994, is now seldom traded in Paris and the 13-year-old futures contract will shut down on May 27, a spokeswoman for the MATIF futures exchange said.
"We are closing it because there are few operators, the market is thinly capitalised and Bintje is now only 30 percent of the market compared to 60 percent a few years ago," she said.
May 27 is the official expiry date for the May contract which currently has 149 lots worth a million francs ($176,000) left open. Contracts with later expiry dates had already been suspended.
The axing of the MATIF contract still leaves potato traders with alternative futures markets in London and Amsterdam.
Potato futures, ignored by all but a few speculators, have seen some of the wildest commodity price swings this decade, turning out fat profits but also enormous risks for investors.
Not covered by the European Union subsidies available to other farm sectors, potato trading is notoriously speculative.
The price for each lot of four 25-kilo bags soared to 317 francs from 60 francs in 1994 and peaked at 341 francs at the beginning of 1995 before plunging just as sharply.
The current price of about 35 francs has been static for months despite fears for a French drought between January and April.
Rains late last month came in time to encourage a healthy new crop and wholesale prices of 7.7 francs a kilo are normal for the time of year, a French potato industry spokeswoman said.
In surreal contrast to hectic scenes at most futures exchanges, however, MATIF's potato trading ring must have qualified as the quietest on earth, even in its heyday.
Cluttered with screens and telephones and looking just like any other futures bearpit, the potato section was occupied by a lone clerk who simply matched prices over the telephone.
There were too few players to justify hiring floor traders and the one-man market was eventually wedged into a corner of the sugar pit to make way for a new futures market in wheat.
In contrast London-based potato futures contracts have a long history of busy trading.
